Title: Distilling the Giant: A Lightweight Command Injection Detection Framework for Grid Edge Networks via LLM-Guided Contrastive Learning
Source title: IET Communications
Abstract: In modern power systems, the communication networks connecting heterogeneous edge devices such as inspection drones and smart charging piles are increasingly targeted by sophisticated, unknown threats, including command injection. While large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated superior semantic capabilities in detecting these complex attacks, their prohibitive computational latency renders them unsuitable for online network defense. To bridge the gap between deep semantic understanding and operational feasibility, we introduce Sentill, a novel framework that distills the reasoning capabilities of giant LLMs into lightweight embedding models. Unlike traditional knowledge distillation that merely mimics output probabilities, Sentill employs a reasoning-aware contrastive learning strategy, aligning the student model's embedding space with the teacher's chain-of-thought (CoT) explanations to capture the underlying logic of attack payloads. Title: Low-Cost Indoor Occupant Localization From Fixed Monocular Cameras Using Architectural Features
Source title: IEEE Access
Abstract: Accurate indoor occupant localization is crucial for occupant-centric building automation, such as activity-aware control and energy optimization. Existing indoor localization solutions commonly rely on stereo cameras, ranging sensors, or wearable devices, which may increase deployment cost, calibration effort, or user intervention. This paper presents a low-cost occupant localization framework using fixed monocular security cameras with stable architectural features to reduce sensing and installation costs. A door frame is used as a metric reference to reduce scene initialization effort and recover occupant position without wearable tags or full-scene dense depth calibration. Two localization pipelines are investigated under the same architectural prior: geometric constraint-based localization (GCL), which uses Perspective-n-Point pose estimation and ground-plane back-projection, and vision-language-model-based localization (VLL), which combines a vision-language model, auxiliary visual encoders, and a position agent. The methods were evaluated with two participants in a residential elevator lobby and a campus corridor under variations in camera viewpoint, positional reference definition, illumination, ground contact visibility, and occupant overlap. Across the evaluated foot-reference, lighting, and multi-occupant conditions, GCL and VLL achieved pooled MAEs of 0.106 m and 0.154 m, respectively, with RMSEs of 0.461 m and 0.198 m for successfully matched occupants. Both methods degraded substantially when the occupant ground contact region was truncated. In the two-occupant experiment, GCL maintains low errors when the architectural reference and occupant foot point are clearly visible, while VLL shows greater sensitivity to image conditions but a smaller error tail. These results demonstrate the feasibility of localization using architectural reference with fixed monocular cameras.  © 2013 IEEE.

Title: An Efficient Finetuning Method for LLM generated text detection in Power Grid

Title: Service Integrity of LLM-Driven Edge Web Services Under Semantic Backdoor Attacks
Source title: Proceedings of the IEEE International Conference on Web Services, ICWS
Abstract: Edge smart-home hubs increasingly rely on frozen Large Language Models (LLMs), customized through third-party Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapters, to perform device control and status reporting. A poisoned adapter, distributed through an open repository, can violate the integrity of LLM-driven edge Web services in two coupled stages: they can first trigger unsafe hardware commands through the service control interface, and then generate benign-looking service responses that misreport the true device state. We study this problem across five opensource models (1B-3B) from the Llama, Qwen, and DeepSeek families, examining how vulnerability varies with model scale, architecture, and reasoning strategy. Our evaluation reveals three key findings. (i) Semantically plausible triggers are far more effective than lexical triggers in this structured service setting. At only 3% poisoning, semantic triggers reach 77.27% unsafeactuation success on Qwen-3B, while lexical triggers remain below 1% under the same conditions. (ii) Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning can reduce semantic backdoor activation at low poisoning ratios, but this protection weakens as poisoning increases. (iii) A poisoned model can conceal unsafe actuation behind benign-looking status reports, with deceptive reporting reaching 96.21% on Llama-3B and 91.00% on Qwen-3B at 10% poisoning. These results show that securing LLM-driven edge Web services requires more than model-level robustness, and CoT reasoning alone is not a reliable safety barrier. Third-party adapters should be audited for hidden backdoor behavior before deployment. Control outputs should be verified against safety constraints at the API boundary before reaching hardware. Most importantly, because poisoned models can mask unsafe states behind plausible reports, the status shown to users must be crosschecked against the actual device state. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: A New Prediction Paradigm for Nonprofessionals: Prompt-based Zero-code Wind Power Prediction
Source title: 2024 6th International Conference on Power and Energy Technology, ICPET 2024
Abstract: Reliable and high-quality wind power prediction results are significant for wind energy utilization and power system management. This article delves into the cutting-edge application of Large Language Models (LLMs) in the domain of wind power generation forecasting, leveraging their zero-shot learning capabilities to circumvent conventional computational constraints. Inspired by the success of language-based pretraining models, this study posits a question: Can these models be adapted to address the challenges of wind power generation forecasting? To examine this, we offer a novel methodology for precise wind power generation forecasting that employs prompt-based techniques. This approach involves converting numerical inputs and outputs into prompts, framing the forecasting task as a conversational interaction. Such a method allows for the direct application of language models in the prediction process. Our findings indicate that, compared to conventional wind power forecasting models, the prompt-based approach offers distinct advantages, particularly when it integrates background knowledge with multivariate inputs. This revolutionary method accelerates the modeling process, decreases the obstacles to adopting complex predictive models, and provides new routes for the research and implementation of renewable energy forecasting. Title: LightLLM4FDD: Domain-specific lightweight large language models for fault detection and diagnosis in building HVAC systems
Source title: Advanced Engineering Informatics
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are an emerging technology with considerable potential for fault detection and diagnosis (FDD) of heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) systems. The local deployment of LLMs serves as an effective strategy to address data security and network availability concerns. However, there is a lack of domain-specific LLMs with both low deployment costs and high FDD performance. To address this gap, a knowledge distillation-based method is proposed to develop a domain-specific lightweight LLM for cost-efficient and high-performance FDD in HVAC systems. The method first establishes a robust knowledge foundation in a lightweight LLM through post–pretraining and supervised fine–tuning on professional documents. It then enables the model to learn the causal relationships between faults and symptoms by supervised fine–tuning on labeled HVAC operating data. For performance evaluation, a domain-specific lightweight LLM is constructed through the two steps: domain adaptation of Llama-3-8B-Instruct using 28 professional documents, followed by supervised fine-tuning on a fault dataset of a single-duct air handling unit (AHU). The proposed method increases the mean diagnosis accuracy of Llama-3-8B-Instruct from 21.0% to 99.8% on the faults of this AHU. The lightweight LLM demonstrates substantially higher mean diagnosis accuracy compared to GPT-4o (68.9%), GPT-5 (79.7%), Claude-Sonnet-4 (69.2%), and DeepSeek-V3 (67.5%). The lightweight LLM is further evaluated on a dual-duct AHU fault dataset. Despite no fine-tuning on this dataset, the lightweight LLM achieves a mean diagnosis accuracy of 98.0%, demonstrating its strong generalization capability. As for deployment costs, the lightweight LLM can run efficiently on accessible consumer-grade GPUs. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Large language models, ChatGPT, and beyond: A new paradigm for condition monitoring and prognosis in power and energy systems
Source title: Energy and AI
Abstract: Large language models and related foundation models offer new capabilities for interpreting heterogeneous information, retrieving engineering knowledge, and supporting high-level decision processes in power and energy systems. This Perspective examines their role in condition monitoring and prognostics and health management, with particular emphasis on remaining useful life estimation. To support language and multimodal model interpretation of structured and validated estimates, we propose a digital twin-centric architecture comprising physics-guided hybrid estimation, digital twin synchronization, rule-governed semantic translation, foundation model reasoning, output validation, and human supervision. The specific contribution is threefold. First, the proposed layering principle distinguishes physically consistent estimation, system integration, and higher-level reasoning functions. Second, an auditable semantic interface is defined to encode health indicators, degradation states, remaining useful life distributions, uncertainty information, operating context, provenance, retrieved evidence, and permitted reasoning scope. Title: Multi-Route Search and Adaptive Fusion for Power QA with Small Language Model Guidance

Authors: Kurzynski M.; Aga S.; Wu D.
Title: Lit Silicon: A Case Where Thermal Imbalance Couples Concurrent Execution in Multiple GPUs
Source title: Proceedings - International Symposium on Computer Architecture
Abstract: GPU systems are increasingly powering modern datacenters at scale. Despite being highly performant, GPU systems can exhibit performance variation at the node and cluster levels. Such performance variation can significantly impact both highperformance computing and artificial intelligence workloads, such as cutting-edge large language models (LLMs). In this work, we analyze the performance of a single-node multi-GPU system running LLM training, and observe that the kernel-level performance variation is highly correlated with concurrent computation and communication (C3), a technique to overlap computation and communication across GPUs for performance gains. We then take a further step to reason that thermally induced straggling coupled with C3 impacts performance variation, which we coin the Lit Silicon effect. More specifically, Lit Silicon describes that in a multi-GPU node, thermal imbalance across GPUs can introduce node-level straggler GPUs (hotter and slower), which in turn slow down the leader GPUs (cooler and faster). Lit Silicon can lead to node-level performance variation and inefficiency, potentially impacting the entire datacenter. We propose analytical performance and power models for Lit Silicon, to understand the potential system-level gains. We further design simple detection and mitigation techniques to effectively address the Lit Silicon problem, and evaluate three different power management solutions, including (1) power optimization under GPU thermal design power, (2) performance optimization under node-level GPU power capping, and (3) performance optimization under node-level CPU power sloshing. We conduct experiments on two workloads on two AMD Instinct™ MI300X GPU systems under two LLM training frameworks, and observe up to 6% performance and 4% power improvements, potentially saving several tens of millions of dollars in electricity costs in datacenters. Our solution consists of approximately 200 lines of PyTorch code, requires no GPU kernel modifications, and can be deployed in datacenters as a new node-level power management layer. Our code is available on GitHub: https://github.com/UnaryLab/lit_silicon_tuning_amd. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: A Reward-Driven Controller for Text Generation with Black-Box Language Models

Abstract: As the primary means of interaction with pretrained language models shifts from local to remote connection, access to fundamental model features such as token embeddings, hidden states, and output probabilities have become restricted. These restrictions reduce the viability of established controllable text generation methods for large language models. To address this, we propose methods for a black-box controller that steers a base language model to generate text possessing a target attribute without relying on any features from the base model. The black-box controller is a pretrained language model fine-tuned using Proximal Policy Optimization to generate a control prefix to guide the generation of a base language model. The controller is evaluated on sentiment control and toxicity avoidance tasks. The results show that the black-box controller is comparable to other controllable text generation baselines in terms of accuracy and diversity of generated text while maintaining high fluency. Title: HALO: A heterogeneous accelerator for low-latency and energy-efficient edge LLM inference
Source title: Future Generation Computer Systems
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference is increasingly deployed in edge-side generative applications. In contrast to cloud-scale inference, which is optimized for large-batch throughput, edge LLM inference operates under a fundamentally different regime characterized by low batch sizes, stringent latency requirements, and tight power budgets. While numerous hardware accelerators have been proposed to improve LLM inference efficiency by optimizing individual components, these designs largely overlook end-to-end systemic bottlenecks specific to low-batch edge execution. As a result, fragmented memory accesses, inefficient nonlinear operator execution, and excessive control overhead remain dominant, severely limiting both latency and energy efficiency in edge systems.To tackle these challenges, we propose HALO, a hardware accelerator architecture specifically designed for low-latency and energy-efficient edge LLM inference. To mitigate bandwidth collapse and energy waste caused by memory fragmentation, HALO introduces a runtime access morphing transfer engine that dynamically coalesces scattered KV cache accesses at runtime. To eliminate the latency and power inefficiency of nonlinear operations, HALO adopts a unified function space projection framework that transforms transcendental functions into linearizable computations executable on high-throughput matrix units. Furthermore, HALO employs a unified execution model that replaces rigid layer-by-layer kernel execution with a persistent computational graph, enabling continuous cross-layer dataflow and eliminating kernel launch overheads. Title: Benchmarking Small Language Models in the Renewable Energy Domain
Source title: Proceedings of the 18th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Utility and Cloud Computing, UCC 2025
Abstract: Small language models (SLMs) are in high demand among utilities in the renewable energy systems domain, as the field is often resource-limited. SLMs enable utilities to deploy functional generative AI capabilities on personal or edge devices, which can greatly assist operators working in remote or rural regions (e.g., wind farms, solar farms, and substations). Nonetheless, the capability and reliability of SLMs in the renewable energy domain remain relatively unexplored, partly due to the lack of proper benchmark datasets to evaluate their effectiveness and accuracy. Title: FDI Attack Detection and LLM-Assisted Resource Allocation for 6G Edge Intelligence-Empowered Distribution Power Grid
Source title: China Communications
Abstract: The intelligent operation management of distribution services is crucial for the stability of power systems. Integrating the large language model (LLM) with 6G edge intelligence provides customized management solutions. However, the adverse effects of false data injection (FDI) attacks on the performance of LLMs cannot be overlooked. Therefore, we propose an FDI attack detection and LLM-assisted resource allocation algorithm for 6G edge intelligence-empowered distribution power grids. First, we formulate a resource allocation optimization problem. The objective is to minimize the weighted sum of the global loss function and total LLM fine-tuning delay under constraints of long-term privacy entropy and energy consumption. Then, we decouple it based on virtual queues. We utilize an LLM-assisted deep Q network (DQN) to learn the resource allocation strategy and design an FDI attack detection mechanism to ensure that fine-tuning remains on the correct path. Title: Context-Aligned Large Language Models for Situational Awareness in Critical Grid Events
Source title: IEEE Green Technologies Conference
Abstract: Power system operators require real-time situational awareness to maintain grid reliability during normal and emergency conditions. During grid emergencies, the operator decision-making process is always high-stakes. Insufficient situational awareness, such as incorrect or untimely responses, can be the cause for major blackouts resulting in adverse impacts on millions of customers as well as huge economic losses. Traditional emergency management systems lack the ability to synthesize multi-source regulatory and operational information during time-critical scenarios. This paper presents a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system for power system operator decision support leveraging a Large Language Model (LLM) with domain-specific knowledge retrieval to address three operational queries: emergency procedure lookup, compliance interpretation, and event response. This involves hybrid retrieval combining sparse and dense searches over local documents, followed by prompting a local quantized LLM. Experimental results indicate that the proposed framework achieves an overall faithfulness of 0.83 and answer relevancy of 0.97, indicating a high degree of potential for improving situational awareness in critical grid operations. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Energy-Aware Code Generation with LLMs: Benchmarking Small vs. Large Language Models for Sustainable AI Programming
Source title: 2025 3rd International Conference on Foundation and Large Language Models, FLLM 2025
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely used for code generation. However, commercial models like ChatGPT require significant computing power, which leads to high energy use and carbon emissions. This has raised concerns about their environmental impact. In this study, we evaluate open-source Small Language Models (SLMs) trained explicitly for code generation and compare their performance and energy efficiency against large LLMs and efficient human-written Python code. The goal is to investigate whether SLMs can match the performance of LLMs on certain types of programming problems while producing more energy-efficient code. We evaluate 150 coding problems from LeetCode, evenly distributed across three difficulty levels: easy, medium, and hard. Our comparison includes three small open-source models, StableCode-3B, StarCoderBase-3B, and Qwen2.5-Coder-3B-Instruct, and two large commercial models, GPT-4.0 and DeepSeek-Reasoner. The generated code is evaluated using four key metrics: run-time, memory usage, energy consumption, and correctness. We use human-written solutions as a baseline to assess the quality and efficiency of the model-generated code. Results indicate that LLMs achieve the highest correctness across all difficulty levels, but SLMs are often more energy-efficient when their outputs are correct. In over 52% of the evaluated problems, SLMs consumed the same or less energy than LLMs. © 2025 IEEE.

Authors: Li X.; Luo F.; Liang R.; Wen S.
Title: A Small-Scale Large Language Model-Enhanced Deep Reinforcement Learning Approach for Prosumer Energy Management
Source title: IEEE Transactions on Consumer Electronics
Abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has been widely applied to tackle energy management tasks and provide real-time decision support. However, existing studies face inherent limitations of DRL methods when required to simultaneously process users’ natural language instructions (NLIs) and optimize control policies in dynamic environments. To address this, a small-scale large language model (LLM)-enhanced DRL approach is proposed to enable the local deployment of LLMs with limited computational resources, thereby improving the agent’s decisionmaking capabilities by effectively utilizing NLIs. Specifically, we fine-tune a small-scale LLM as an information processor to deal with various NLIs for the operation and settings of heating, ventilation, and air conditioning systems and battery energy storage systems. The model summarizes the NLIs into structured text, which is then converted into embeddings. We design a trainable feature extractor to capture representative features from the embeddings, providing extra inputs for the agent. To effectively utilize the representative features, we introduce an action alteration network and a critic alteration network, providing explicit adjustments to the traditional actor-critic algorithm. Finally, we apply the proposed method to address a non-convex energy management problem. Case studies show that the small-scale LLM-enhanced DRL method can reduce energy costs by at least 13.7% compared to benchmark methods. © 1975-2011 IEEE.

Title: Instant Segmentation for IoT-Enabled Smart-Grid Networks with a Hybrid Small Language Model Policy Selection
Source title: Conference Proceedings - IEEE SOUTHEASTCON
Abstract: As a key technology that enabled the evolution of traditional grids to next generation smart grids, internet of things has also enabled smart grids to have an expanded attack surface. This paper addresses the problem that Internet of Things are not given immediate network cybersecurity defenses once joining a smart grid which is a major vulnerability. The proposed hybrid machine learning and deep learning-based autonomous decision-making system framework will focus on implementing instant network segmentation configurations deduced from IoT sensor data and network telemetry data. This system is evaluated on a framework that utilizes a testbed that involves network telemetry data relating to cyber-attacks while utilizing a GPT-2-based small language model implemented using the HuggingFace Transformers framework. The hybrid model performed well overall for the logistic regression model and small language model. Results show a near-perfect ROC-AUC performance across evaluated attack classes from the logistic regression models, while the small language model has a perplexity of 1.02 and a TPOT of 31.6 nanoseconds indicating it is very confident and timely in the next token selection. This study supports the concept that instant network segmentation can be achieved for Internet of Thingsenabled smart grids with autonomous network-based defense mechanisms. In this context, 'instant' refers to near-real-time policy selection following packet-level inference without human intervention. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: A Low-Rank Enhanced Lightweight Multimodal LLM Framework for Efficient Edge Power Visual Detection
Source title: Conference Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Systems, Man and Cybernetics
Abstract: With the development of artificial intelligence, many visual detection methods have been applied to power systems. However, diverse tasks cause existing solutions to face low detection accuracy and resource constraints in edge power scenarios. In this paper, we propose a low-rank enhanced lightweight multimodal LLM framework for efficient edge power visual detection. The framework can effectively balance the model performance with the resource constraints of edge deployment by introducing multimodal LLM and fusing data augmentation strategies and low-rank optimization. First, to enhance the adaptability of diverse visual detection tasks, we design a diverse data augmentation strategy for multimodal LLM to solve the problem of insufficient power scene data. Then, we reduce the number of training parameters by a low-rank optimization technique to enable the model to run efficiently on resource-limited edge devices. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed framework can improve the accuracy by more than 3% on average under different power visual detection tasks. It can also save 76.49% of graphics memory consumption and accelerate training by 81.88%. © 2025 IEEE.

Title: A Generalized Framework of Large Language Models for Power System Operation: Implementations and Limitations

Abstract: In recent years, the rapid development of smart grid technologies and energy markets has brought massive new entities into the power system, such as virtual power plant (VPP) operators, distribution retailers, electric vehicle (EV) aggregators, and end prosumers. These entities with little knowledge of power system modeling, dispatch, and optimization require a more intelligent and flexible approach to ensure their efficient participation. Trained on a vast corpus of text data, generative pre-trained transformer (GPT) based large language models (LLMs) are embedded with massive world knowledge. With powerful comprehension and reasoning capabilities, GPT based LLMs have the potential to enable intelligent and customized dispatch. However, despite extensive experimentation, existing studies have neither addressed how LLMs should be applied in power systems nor provided a generalized framework. In this paper, we propose a generalized framework of LLMs for power system operation and discuss its implementations and limitations in detail. Comprehensive case studies and test results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework and several critical factors to ensure the performance of LLMs. © 2025 IEEE.

Title: Integrating LLMs into Smart Home Architecture: Design, Implementation, and Experimental Insights
Source title: 5th IEEE International Conference on Mobile Networks and Wireless Communications, ICMNWC 2025
Abstract: Smart home systems are a key application of the Internet of Things (IoT) paradigm. These devices are either directly or indirectly connected to a network in order to perceive actions based on user willingness or sensing. As Information and Communication Technology (ICT) advances, Large Language Models (LLMs) are growing increasingly potent. Agents with LLM capabilities could be very supportive for smart home systems because of their natural language comprehension. In this paper, we introduce an LLM-powered smart home agent with real-time connectivity to smart home devices. This proposal has been experimented with and evaluated with typical smart home use cases. This experimental architecture illustrates a realtime scenario of a standard smart home, where sensors, lights, and switches are interconnected in a multi-tiered environment. The sensor, gateway, and switch modules are connected to the smart home edge server via a Web of Things (WoT) interface. The experiment has been conducted with various types of smart home use case prompts, including status requests, control requests, automation requests, and reasoning requests. The outcome of the experiment indicates that the addition of LLM to smart homes excels in natural conversational patterns compared to keywordbased agents. The prompt response time, which is unsuitable for time-sensitive tasks like anomaly detection, is a drawback, and edge LLMs could be a solution.  © 2025 IEEE.
